feed.title: Quantum Landmines and Vulnerable Coin Auctions

entry.title: Quantum Landmines and Vulnerable Coin Auctions
entry.summary:
The concept of using a "landmine" as purposeful bait in the context of quantum attacks on Bitcoin introduces an intriguing dynamic. By making it impossible to determine which coins are quantum-safe at any given time, this approach effectively undermines arguments for freezing vulnerable coins. The uncertainty surrounding the security of any unspent transaction output (UTXO), including those belonging to Satoshi, means that their vulnerability only becomes apparent during an actual theft attempt. In this sense, UTXO superposition serves as an unexpected form of defense against quantum threats.
The idea of incentivizing users not to move coins initially appears counterintuitive. However, reframing the situation reveals that coins are essentially "moved" when the landmine is deployed, as they become protected and remain spendable by the owner, though this protection is not externally observable. Depending on the evolution of network forking and migration processes, such a mechanism could be advantageous or detrimental. This approach stands out as there have been few, if any, proposals aiming to invert the typical relationship with quantum attackers, allowing them to exist but discouraging attacks through economic disincentives.
The broader question revolves around which on-chain transactions should be incentivized. Rather than focusing solely on transactional incentives, these thought experiments consider whether coexistence with an active quantum attacker is possible while preserving Bitcoin’s foundational principles. The most ideologically aligned solutions appear to involve imposing financial penalties for theft and offering rewards for defending the blockchain from attacks, both of which are facilitated by the landmine strategy.
Recovery schemes, traditionally seen as safety mechanisms, may also benefit from being expanded into proactive offensive and defensive tools. By integrating the same collateral rules used in landmines, recovery strategies could alter participant incentives more fundamentally. While the practical implementation and the potential impact on migration are still open questions, this line of thinking presents a novel method for enhancing Bitcoin's resilience in the face of quantum adversaries. For further discussions and insights, readers can refer to the [Bitcoin Development Mailing List](https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/bitcoin-dev).
